name: Hamtramck Enclave
description:
Hamtramck has always been an enclave — a 2.1-square-mile city entirely surrounded by Detroit, stubbornly independent since 1922 when it incorporated to avoid Detroit's prohibition enforcement. A century and a half later, the stubbornness remains, though what it's resisting has changed. Hamtramck Enclave is one of the most ethnically dense districts in the GLMZ: Bangladeshi, Yemeni, Polish, Bosnian, and a dozen other communities layered on top of each other in a geography so compact that you can walk from a mosque to a pierogi shop to a Yemeni tea house in four minutes. The neural interfaces are older models here. The streets are narrower. The buildings are not optimized. Nobody asked them to be.

The Enclave's legal status is a relic that the corponations have been trying to dissolve for forty years. As an incorporated municipality predating the Corporate Sovereignty Acts, Hamtramck retains its own city charter, its own police force (twelve officers, three functional patrol vehicles, and a determination that exceeds their equipment), and its own zoning authority. This makes it a jurisdictional island — corporate law stops at the border, and the corporations hate it. Three separate acquisition attempts have failed, not because of legal challenges but because the Enclave's population voted them down with margins exceeding 85%. The corponations could force the issue — the legal mechanisms exist — but the optics of dissolving an immigrant community's century-old charter are bad enough that nobody wants to be the one who does it. Yet.

What the Enclave has become, in practice, is a refuge for people who need to exist outside corporate jurisdiction without going fully off-grid. Small businesses that can't afford corporate licensing operate here. Augment technicians who lost their certifications but not their skills practice here. Religious communities that refuse to allow neural interface monitoring during worship gather here. The Enclave is not ungoverned — it is self-governed, badly funded, overextended, and alive in the particular way that places are alive when the people who live there actually chose to be there.

sights: Dense streets where mosque minarets, church steeples, and apartment blocks compete for skyline in two square miles
Shop signs in Bengali, Arabic, Polish, Bosnian, English, and combinations that only make sense locally
The old Hamtramck police station — a building from 2119 that looks ancient next to everything else and still works
Prayer rugs drying on fire escapes next to satellite dishes jury-rigged to pull signals the corporate net doesn't carry
Children from six ethnic backgrounds playing the same game in a language they invented together
sounds: Five call-to-prayer speakers and three church bells sharing the same airspace — a theological soundscape
Conversations in languages that shift mid-sentence — Hamtramck's polyglot baseline
The Enclave police scanner — twelve officers trying to cover 2.1 square miles with optimism and determination
Unlicensed augment shop equipment humming behind residential walls — everyone knows, nobody reports
Kitchen sounds from every open window — the Enclave cooks constantly and competitively
smells: Layered cuisine — Yemeni spices, Polish sausage, Bangladeshi curry, Bosnian cevapi, all within a single block's airspace
Incense from the religious supply shops that serve every faith represented in the Enclave
Old buildings — plaster, wood, the accumulated smell of a century of human habitation in compact spaces
Tea. Every community here runs on tea, and the varieties would fill a catalog.
atmosphere.feel: Cramped, loud, genuine, and defiantly human. Hamtramck Enclave feels like what a city is supposed to feel like before the optimization algorithms get involved. It's messy. The infrastructure creaks. The politics are personal. And the community cohesion — forged from a dozen different cultures deciding that their differences matter less than their shared refusal to be absorbed — is the strongest thing in Detroit that isn't made of steel.

demographics: Approximately 32,000 residents in 2.1 square miles — one of the highest population densities in the GLMZ. Bangladeshi (28%), Yemeni (22%), Polish (15%), Bosnian (12%), and a patchwork of other communities. Median age: 34. The Enclave's birth rate is the highest in the Detroit metro area, which the corponations view as a resource problem and the residents view as a future.
economy: Small-business intensive. Approximately 1,200 businesses in 2.1 square miles — restaurants, shops, unlicensed augment technicians, religious supply stores, and informal services. Annual economic output: Φ4.2 billion, almost entirely circulated internally. The Enclave pays for municipal services through a property tax that hasn't been raised since 2181 and is increasingly insufficient.
power_structure: Elected city council of seven members representing ward districts. The mayor, currently Fatima Al-Rashidi, has held office for nine years and governs through coalition-building across ethnic community leaders. The twelve-officer police force reports to the council. Corporate influence is present through property purchases on the border but has not penetrated the governance structure. Yet.
dangers: Incorporation pressure — the next corporate acquisition attempt is always being planned
Infrastructure decay — the Enclave's independent infrastructure is aging and underfunded
Internal ethnic tensions — the coalition holds but is not frictionless, especially around resource allocation
Border exploitation — corporate interests buy border properties and use them to project influence inward
Medical limitations — the Enclave's clinic cannot handle advanced augment complications, forcing residents into corporate medical systems
opportunities: Jurisdictional sanctuary — the Enclave's independent charter makes it a legal safe harbor from corporate authority
Unlicensed but skilled augment work — the technicians here are good, cheap, and don't ask questions
Intelligence network — the Enclave's polyglot, multi-ethnic community has connections across the GLMZ and internationally
Cultural community trust — earn standing in one community and the word spreads to the others
story_hooks: A corponation has purchased seven properties on the Enclave's western border and is quietly building a sensor network — if they can prove the Enclave can't maintain public safety standards, they have legal grounds to petition for dissolution

An unlicensed augment technician in the Enclave has developed a firmware patch that blocks Tessera's neural data harvesting. Tessera wants the technician. The Enclave wants to protect them. The technician wants to sell to the highest bidder.

Mayor Al-Rashidi receives a private offer: accept a 'partnership' with Cinderblock AI that preserves the Enclave's charter in name while transferring operational authority. The alternative is a hostile acquisition vote at the next GLMZ Council session.
frequented_by: Residents who chose the Enclave because it's outside the system
Unlicensed augment clients from across Detroit
Corporate scouts mapping the Enclave's vulnerabilities

notable_locations.name: The Bazaar Block
notable_locations.description: A single city block containing 47 businesses from 11 ethnic backgrounds — the densest commercial district in the GLMZ

notable_locations.name: Hamtramck Community Clinic
notable_locations.description: Volunteer-staffed medical facility that handles everything from broken bones to basic augment maintenance — overwhelmed, essential, and running on donated supplies

notable_locations.name: The Assembly Hall
notable_locations.description: Former auto union meeting hall, now the Enclave's civic center — where city council meets, community disputes are mediated, and acquisition resistance is coordinated
